messages.content:
Compute the largest positive integer \( n \) such that

\[
n \text{ divides } (\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor)!^{n!} + 450.
\]

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let  
\[
m=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor,\qquad E=n!.
\]
So \(m^2\le n<(m+1)^2\), and the expression is
\[
(m!)^{n!}+450.
\]

We analyze divisibility prime power by prime power. Let \(p^a\Vert n\) be the exact prime power dividing \(n\).

### 1. Primes \(p\le m\)

If \(p\le m\), then \(p\mid m!\), so
\[
(m!)^{n!}\equiv 0\pmod{p^a}
\]
because \(v_p((m!)^{n!})=n!\,v_p(m!)\ge a\). Therefore \(p^a\mid 450\).

Since
\[
450=2\cdot 3^2\cdot 5^2,
\]
the only possible prime powers coming from \(p\le m\) are
\[
2,\quad 3,\ 9,\quad 5,\ 25.
\]

### 2. Primes \(p>m\)

If \(p>m\), then \(\gcd(m!,p)=1\). Also \(p^a\mid n\), so \(p^a\le n\), and
\[
\varphi(p^a)=p^{a-1}(p-1)\le p^a\le n.
\]
Thus \(\varphi(p^a)\mid n!\), so by Euler’s theorem,
\[
(m!)^{n!}\equiv 1\pmod{p^a}.
\]
Hence we need
\[
p^a\mid 1+450=451.
\]
But
\[
451=11\cdot 41.
\]
Thus the only possible prime powers from \(p>m\) are
\[
11,\quad 41.
\]
Moreover, if \(11\mid n\), then \(11>m\), so \(m<11\), giving \(n<121\).  
If \(41\mid n\), then \(41>m\), so \(m<41\), giving \(n<1681\).

Therefore every valid \(n\) has the form
\[
n=2^a3^b5^c11^d41^e
\]
with
\[
a\le 1,\quad b\le 2,\quad c\le 2,\quad d,e\le 1.
\]

Now maximize.

- If \(41\mid n\), then \(n<1681\), and \(11\nmid n\) (otherwise \(n\ge 41\cdot 11=451>120\)). So
  \[
  n=41t,\qquad t\mid 450,\qquad t<41.
  \]
  The largest divisor of \(450\) below \(41\) is \(30\). Thus
  \[
  n\le 41\cdot 30=1230.
  \]

- If \(11\mid n\) but \(41\nmid n\), then \(n<121\), so
  \[
  n=11t,\quad t\mid 450,\quad t<11.
  \]
  The largest such \(t\) is \(10\), giving \(n\le 110\).

- If neither \(11\) nor \(41\) divides \(n\), then \(n\mid 450\), so \(n\le 450\).

Hence every valid \(n\le 1230\).

Finally, check that \(n=1230\) works. We have
\[
1230=2\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 41,\qquad \lfloor\sqrt{1230}\rfloor=35.
\]
Modulo \(2,3,5\), both \(35!\) and \(450\) are \(0\), so those prime factors divide the expression.

Modulo \(41\), since \(41\nmid 35!\) and \(40\mid 1230!\),
\[
(35!)^{1230!}\equiv 1\pmod{41},
\]
and
\[
1+450=451\equiv 0\pmod{41}.
\]
Thus \(2,3,5,41\) all divide the expression, so \(1230\) divides it.

Therefore the largest such integer is

\[
\boxed{1230}
\]
